title: Council responds to Ontario's Bill 23 housing legislation
subtitle: Inclusionary zoning deferred, climate advocacy, 2023 user fees, natural gas and water rates, capital pre-approvals, Centre in the Square appointments.
overview: Council spent most of this special meeting on Bill 23, the provincial More Homes Built Faster Act. It asked staff for an implementation plan covering Bill 23 and two earlier housing laws, due by June 26, 2023. Council also backed the Ontario Big City Mayors' advocacy resolution, which asks the province to pause changes to development charges and parkland fees, and to make municipalities whole for lost revenue. A climate-focused resolution also asked the province to pause Bill 23. Staff said the 2023 budget has not been changed for Bill 23's financial effects, and that they plan to address them through the 2024 budget.
Council deferred a motion on inclusionary zoning, which would ask the province to reconsider its affordable-unit rules, until staff report back in the first half of 2023.

Council also approved most 2023 user fees, with planning fees and two engineering fees put off to December 19. It approved water rates and a lower natural gas supply rate from January 1, 2023, pre-approved 2023 capital projects for early procurement, and appointed two members to the Centre in the Square board. After a closed session, Council authorized an Ontario Land Tribunal settlement agreement; the minutes do not publicly report its terms.

decisions.detail: Staff were directed to prepare an implementation action plan for Bill 23 and the earlier Bill 13 and Bill 109, and report back by June 26, 2023 {{vote:m1}}.

Council endorsed the Ontario Big City Mayors' requests to pause development charge and parkland fee changes, make municipalities whole dollar-for-dollar, and set shared accountability and targets for all housing partners; it was carried unanimously.
Council asked the province to pause Bill 23 (amended from a request to repeal it), analyse the economic cost of climate disasters, and work with municipalities on local efficiencies {{vote:m4}}.
A motion asking the province to rethink its inclusionary zoning rules was deferred to a Council meeting no later than June 2023, so staff can await further provincial regulations {{vote:m3}}.
Council approved the 2023 user fee schedule, except planning fees and two engineering fees, which were deferred to the December 19, 2022 meeting {{vote:m7}}.
The supply component of Kitchener Utilities' natural gas rate was lowered to 20.85 cents per cubic metre from 21.45, with delivery rates approved and supply to be reviewed quarterly {{vote:m9}}.
Council pre-approved the listed 2023 capital projects for procurement before the 2023 budget is passed {{vote:m6}}.
The General Manager of Development Services was authorized to sign a Memorandum of Understanding on an Ontario Land Tribunal matter, to the City Solicitor's satisfaction {{vote:m11}}.

debate: The Mayor said the Big City Mayors considered asking the province to repeal Bill 23 but judged repeal unlikely, so the group focused on areas where change seemed achievable. He asked Council to pass the motion unamended so municipalities speak with one voice.

Several councillors supported the Big City Mayors motion as a partnership approach, while one asked how smaller municipalities and groups calling for repeal were represented. The Mayor pointed to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario and the Big City Mayors caucus as the main channels. One councillor noted that taxpayers may still bear costs even if the province makes cities whole.

On inclusionary zoning, supporters of deferral said asking the province to change the rules was premature before staff finish their analysis and provincial regulations are released. Others pointed to rising homelessness and urged speed. Staff said a report is aimed for late in the first quarter of 2023 and that market-based affordability definitions concern them.

A delegate urged Council to ask for Bill 23 to be repealed, citing climate commitments, farmland and the Greenbelt. Council staff advised that a repeal request would contradict the earlier motion, so the climate motion was changed to ask for a pause. A councillor withdrew a motion to reconsider after learning a failed reconsideration would block a later repeal motion this term.
Councillors supporting the climate motion cited groundwater, farmland and wetlands. One said it avoids pitting climate against housing supply by asking the province to pursue both goals.
